newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Busang shock seen threat to small miners in Africa.
newsitem.headline: Busang shock seen threat to small miners in Africa.

text.p: Junior mining companies, hit by Indonesia's Busang gold scandal, will find it much harder to raise capital for African projects in future, leaving majors to scoop up prospects on the cheap, analysts said on Monday.
Due to its lack of infrastructure and political risk, Africa is expensive to mine and small Canadian and Australian companies exploring the continent have mostly operated on tight budgets.

Now those small players are likely to take a hammering as investors give them a wide berth in the wake of the Busang catastrophe, which earlier on Monday was said to be the biggest fraud in the history of mining.

What could have been the century's biggest gold find by Canada's Bre-X Minerals Ltd of 71 million ounces deep in Borneo's jungles, is now said to be uneconomic after consultants Strathcona Mineral Services Ltd said they found evidence of tampering with Busang core samples.

Recent panic-selling of shares in small mining firms is likely to slow but analysts say the Busang bombshell is compounded by a lacklustre bullion and does not bode well for those companies that dashed into Africa to compete with majors.
"One of the consequences of Busang will be that majors will be able to pick up projects from juniors at bargain-basement prices," said Barry Sergeant, analyst at BOE Natwest.
Analysts say investment banks could also become reluctant to fund juniors and this would leave the continent wide open to giant mining companies with their own capital resources.
"It will give the majors a bigger piece of the action because they can weather the storm," said Trevor Pearton, head of mining research at Societe Generale Frankel Pollak.
Funding aside, exploration costs are also likely to swell.

Stock markets worldwide will call for tighter regulation to avoid a repeat of Busang, analysts said. This will raise exploration costs as companies are forced to drill repeatedly and conduct independent evaluations to meet standards.
"Regulations will be very tough on small miners. They're on a shoe-string budget most of the time. This (stricter regulations) could slow the procedure," Pearton said.
Bre-X is listed in Toronto and analysts say Canadian reporting standards can be held responsible for investors losing money in the Busang scam.

"Juniors can report more ounces in Canada than anywhere else -- gold reserves, measured resources and inferred resources -- whereas in the U.S. only proven and probable reserves are allowed to be reported," Sergeant said.
The Toronto Stock Exchange and Ontario Securities Commission in April set up a task force to study tougher mining rules.
Analysts say that it is increasingly expensive to bring an ounce of gold resource (deposit) to the status of gold reserve (proven and probable).
"These days it costs between $30 and $40 an ounce. The juniors just don't have that money," Sergeant said.
African mining exploration is also heading into a new era as most previous exploration has focused on areas of known gold history, like abandoned colonial mines.
But these sites are already in hand and any future exploration is likely to be in virgin territory, analysts said.
Without the security of knowing the site was once a mine, juniors are increasingly unlikely to take on uncharted territory with Busang hanging over them, they added.
